title: Source Code and Running Program
definition: Source code is a human-authored program representation; a running program is the dynamic execution of a translated or interpreted representation within an execution environment.
purpose: Prevent learners from treating a file on disk and its evolving runtime behavior as the same object.
history: Stored-program computers and successive language abstractions separated human-facing notation from machine execution; this chapter uses only the conceptual distinction.
mental_model: A recipe is a representation; a cooking session is an unfolding process with tools, ingredients, and changing state.
analogy: The recipe/cooking analogy clarifies representation versus process but fails where humans infer missing instructions that machines cannot safely infer.
real_world_usage: Distinguishing a source repository from a deployed process
Explaining why the same source may behave differently across environments
common_mistakes: Calling an unopened source file a running process
Assuming every language uses one fixed translation pipeline
industry_notes: Build, deployment, and runtime diagnostics operate on different artifacts and must preserve version identity.
ai_notes: AI-generated source must still be translated, executed, tested, and observed; plausible text is not runtime evidence.
interview_notes: Ask the candidate to distinguish source, executable representation, process, and output without requiring one language implementation.
exercise_candidates: Classify source file, executable artifact, process, and output in two environments
lab_candidates: Compare a source edit before and after restarting a running process
project_candidates: Annotate the stages of a tiny instruction simulator
